#8484. QuickBooks Online Review – The Accounting Software Your Accountant Knows, at a Higher Price

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Choose QuickBooks Online if your accountant already works in it or your business tracks inventory or projects. Plans with accountant access cost $38 to $340 a month after three discounted months, so if you mostly send invoices, a cheaper plan or app does that for less.

Picking accounting software is mostly a decision about who else will work in your books. If a bookkeeper or accountant closes your books each month or files your business return, using the program they already know saves time on both sides. If nobody else logs in, you pay for collaboration you never use.

QuickBooks Online is the cloud accounting software Intuit sells to small businesses. Intuit, founded in 1983 and based in Mountain View, California, also makes TurboTax and says about 100 million customers use its products. It says 650,000 accountants worldwide use its platform, and every plan from Simple Start up includes free logins for two or three of yours. QuickBooks customers are also paying more. Intuit’s fiscal 2026 results, for the year that ended July 31, 2026, show QuickBooks Online Accounting revenue up 23%. Intuit said the fourth quarter’s 20% gain came from customers paying more on average, more customers, and changes in which plans they buy.

QuickBooks Online comes in six plans. QuickBooks Free and QuickBooks Lite are for one person working alone, while the four business plans, Simple Start through Advanced, add accountant access and, from Essentials up, more users. Each business plan includes everything in the one below it, so your choice comes down to how many people need logins and whether you track inventory or projects.

New customers on a monthly plan choose between 50% off for 3 months and a 30-day free trial, then pay the plan’s current price each month until they cancel, with no annual contract. By our math, the discount saves $70 in year one. Over the first 12 months, Plus costs $1,470 with it (three months at $70, then nine at $140) and $1,540 with the trial (11 paid months at $140).

Not every business needs Simple Start. If you mostly send invoices, QuickBooks Lite handles them for $20 a month without accountant access, and Wave’s free Starter plan covers unlimited invoices, estimates, bills, and bookkeeping records. If your team needs more logins but no inventory tracking, compare Xero, which charges no per-user license fees.

Every plan pulls in transactions from the bank and card accounts you connect, one bank on Free and two on Lite. From Simple Start up, QuickBooks copies the categories you choose and applies them to new transactions automatically. Intuit Intelligence, Intuit’s name for its AI tools, does more at each level:

Intuit still calls Intuit Intelligence a beta release, so its features and limits can change. You choose which tasks run on their own and can undo what the AI did. Only admin users get the chat, and each plan caps how much they can use it each month.

QuickBooks Free caps invoices at two a month unless you qualify for and turn on QuickBooks Payments, which lets customers pay an invoice by card or bank transfer. Payments has no monthly fee, but each transaction costs:

Bill pay comes with every business plan. Intuit’s plan pages list five free standard ACH bill payments a month, an allotment they say may vary, and $0.50 for each one after that. Its Bill Pay page calls standard ACH free on every plan, so confirm the fee with Intuit before you pay more than five vendors a month that way. Checks cost $1.50, and Faster ACH, which usually arrives the next business day, costs $10. For $15 a month, Bill Pay Premium adds AI bill entry and unlimited e-filing of the 1099 forms you send contractors. Bill Pay Elite, at $45 a month, adds approval workflows and user roles, and it has come free with Advanced since Aug. 1, 2026.

Inventory and job costing start at Plus. Plus updates quantities on hand automatically, alerts you when an item needs reordering, drafts purchase orders, and turns them into bills when the goods arrive. Its project tools track labor, payroll, and expenses for each job, and it adds budgets and up to 40 classes and locations for sorting income and expenses. Advanced lifts that limit and adds custom reports and dashboards, two-way syncing with Excel, and an estimates-versus-actuals report for projects.

No QuickBooks Online plan includes payroll. Intuit sells it separately as QuickBooks Workforce, at a monthly base fee plus a fee for each employee:

New customers pay half the base fee for three months, but per-employee fees stay at full price. At full price, a five-person team on Workforce Payroll pays $85 a month, $50 plus $35 in employee fees.

Expert Assisted, at $59 a month after a 30-day free trial, gives you a bookkeeping expert to answer questions but not to work in your books. Full-Service Bookkeeping, with a dedicated bookkeeper doing the monthly work, starts at $300 a month after a one-time cleanup fee, and a cleanup alone starts at $600. Neither service prepares or files your taxes.

Phone support comes with every business plan and is free during the trial, while QuickBooks Free gets chat. Advanced adds Priority Circle, a premium support line with on-demand training. The Better Business Bureau (BBB) gives Intuit an F, citing complaints it failed to answer or resolve. It logged more than 4,600 complaints against Intuit in the last three years, nearly 2,000 of them in the past 12 months. Those counts cover all of Intuit’s products, TurboTax and Mailchimp included, not QuickBooks alone.

Leaving QuickBooks takes planning. The Export data tool saves your reports and lists to a single .zip of Excel files. Estimates, purchase orders, attachments, and your chart of accounts (the list of categories your books use) export separately, and Intuit’s help page names two ways out, Excel or QuickBooks Desktop. After you cancel a paid plan, you keep read-only access for a year to finish exporting. Cancel during or after a free trial, and Intuit keeps your data for 90 days.

QuickBooks Online is the safe pick when someone besides you works in the books. Your accountant gets in free, Plus handles inventory and job costing, and the account grows to 25 users on Advanced without a move. On the higher plans, its AI now does real cleanup and reconciliation work.

It’s poor value for a one-person business that mostly sends invoices. Simple Start’s $38 a month buys accountant access and reports that business won’t use, while QuickBooks Lite handles invoicing for $20 and Wave for nothing. The discounted price also doubles after the third month, and payroll costs extra. If your accountant already works in QuickBooks, pick the plan that covers your headcount and budget for its full price from the fourth month.

#8483. Solo Health Review (2026): Costs, Coverage, Pros & Cons

If you’re self-employed, finding affordable health coverage can be challenging. Traditional health insurance premiums can take a big bite out of your budget, especially when you’re paying for coverage without employer help.

Solo Health offers a different approach to health coverage designed specifically for entrepreneurs, freelancers, and self-employed business owners. Instead of purchasing a traditional individual health insurance policy, eligible business owners establish a self-funded major medical plan through their business.

But how does Solo Health work? Is the coverage comprehensive? And could it actually save you money? In this Solo Health review, we’ll break down the costs, benefits, potential drawbacks, and important details you should understand before enrolling.

Solo Health is a health coverage solution designed for self-employed individuals and business owners who want an alternative to traditional individual health insurance.

The company offers self-funded major medical plans that provide access to healthcare services through a nationwide PPO provider network.

Unlike a traditional insurance policy purchased through the Affordable Care Act (ACA) Marketplace, Solo Health uses a business-based structure.

Your business establishes its own self-funded health plan to cover eligible medical claims.

According to Solo Health, its plans include:

One of Solo Health’s biggest selling points is major medical coverage specifically designed for self-employed people.

However, Solo Health is not a traditional ACA Marketplace insurance policy, and eligibility depends on a health questionnaire.

Solo Health operates differently from both traditional health insurance and healthcare-sharing programs. Instead of purchasing an individual insurance policy, your business establishes a self-funded health plan.

That self-funded plan pays eligible medical claims under the terms of your plan documents.

Here’s a simplified overview of how it works:

Preventive care is generally covered without meeting your deductible.

Prescription medications have their own coverage rules, including copays after the deductible.

Solo Health describes its product as a self-funded major medical health plan, not a healthcare-sharing ministry or a conventional individual insurance policy.

Eligible medical claims are paid through your business’s self-funded health plan.

While Solo Health provides major medical benefits, you should not assume it has all the same eligibility protections, regulatory requirements, or consumer safeguards as an ACA-compliant individual insurance policy.

For example, Solo Health requires applicants to complete a health questionnaire and meet its participation requirements. This differs significantly from ACA Marketplace plans, which generally cannot reject applicants because of preexisting medical conditions.

Before enrolling, make sure you understand the plan documents, coverage exclusions, and how the plan pays medical claims.

Solo Health offers several key medical benefits designed to protect members from both routine healthcare expenses and larger medical bills.

Here’s a closer look at what is included.

Solo Health covers eligible preventive healthcare services at 100%, with no deductible required.

This can be particularly helpful for self-employed individuals who want to stay on top of their health without paying the full cost of every preventive appointment. However, diagnostic tests or treatments performed during a preventive visit may be billed differently.

Solo Health covers primary care physicians and medical specialists. Members can access participating providers through the MultiPlan PHCS network, now associated with Claritev.

You generally don’t need a referral to see a specialist. For most non-preventive visits, you’ll pay the applicable cost until you meet your deductible. After you meet your deductible, the plan covers eligible medical services at 100%, subject to plan terms.

One of the most important reasons to have health coverage is protection against unexpected medical emergencies. A serious accident, hospitalization, or surgery can result in tens of thousands of dollars in medical bills.

According to the company, emergency services are processed as in-network regardless of which hospital provides the care.

Certain planned hospital admissions and surgeries require prior authorization.

Solo Health covers eligible mental health and substance use treatment. This can include outpatient therapy and other qualifying services. However, limits apply.

For example, Solo Health limits outpatient mental health therapy to 40 visits per covered individual each year. Some mental health treatments may also require prior authorization. If you regularly use mental health services, review these limitations before enrolling.

Solo Health includes prescription benefits administered through FairosRx. Preventive medications in Tier 1 are covered at $0. For other covered medications, members generally pay the discounted cost until they meet their deductible.

Afterward, prescription copays apply based on the medication’s tier. Some specialty medications can still involve high out-of-pocket costs.

Solo Health also lists maternity and newborn care among its covered benefits. This can include eligible prenatal services, childbirth, and medical care for newborns.

However, anyone planning to start or expand a family should review the plan’s maternity provisions, eligibility requirements, and applicable exclusions before enrolling. Don’t assume every pregnancy-related service will automatically qualify for payment.

One of the biggest questions when considering any health coverage option is how much you’ll pay. Solo Health offers three plan designs, each with a different deductible.

The main difference between these plans is how much you must pay toward eligible medical expenses before the plan pays most covered costs at 100%.

All three plans offer the same core coverage and provider network. The deductible you select influences your monthly payment. Generally speaking, plans with lower deductibles cost more per month, while plans with higher deductibles cost less.

Your actual monthly cost depends on factors such as your age, location, household composition, and eligibility. Because pricing is individualized, the best way to determine your cost is to request a quote directly from Solo Health.

Let’s say you choose the Solo Health plan with a $5,000 individual deductible. You would generally pay the applicable cost of eligible non-preventive healthcare services until you’ve spent $5,000 toward your deductible.

After that, the plan pays 100% of eligible medical expenses for the remainder of the plan year. However, prescription copays and potential out-of-network charges can still apply.

This is why it’s important to understand the difference between your deductible and your total possible healthcare expenses.

Solo Health advertises its deductible as the out-of-pocket maximum for eligible medical care.

This structure can make medical expenses easier to plan for.

However, the advertised maximum may not cover every expense you could incur.

Prescription copays, excluded services, and charges above the plan’s out-of-network reimbursement amount may result in additional costs.

When comparing plans, consider both your monthly payments and what you could reasonably afford if you had a major medical event.

Solo Health uses a six-tier prescription drug structure. Here is the company’s published schedule for covered medications after meeting the deductible.

Tier 1 preventive medications are available without meeting the deductible. For most other covered prescriptions, these copays apply after the deductible is satisfied. The plan also restricts certain expensive medications.

For example, the plan may exclude non-specialty medications that exceed specified price thresholds. If you take prescription medications regularly, check the company’s formulary to confirm whether your medications are covered and what they might cost.

A Health Savings Account (HSA) can be a valuable tool for managing healthcare expenses. HSAs can offer tax advantages when you contribute, invest, and use the funds for qualified medical expenses.

According to Solo Health’s published FAQ, the V2500 and V5000 plan designs are HSA-eligible, while the V10000 plan is not currently listed as HSA-eligible. However, HSA eligibility depends on federal tax requirements, not simply a plan’s marketing designation.

Before contributing, confirm that your specific coverage qualifies as an HSA-compatible high-deductible health plan under current IRS rules. This matters because deductible amounts alone don’t establish HSA eligibility.

Customer experiences can provide valuable insight when evaluating a healthcare company. However, a company’s advertised benefits differ from what customers experience when submitting medical claims.

Solo Health publishes information about its coverage, member services, and claims administration. It also offers concierge assistance and an online member portal.

Solo Health offers several features that may appeal to certain self-employed individuals.

Many freelancers and small business owners don’t have access to employer-sponsored health insurance. Solo Health is specifically designed for people in this situation.

Its business-based structure gives qualifying entrepreneurs another option to consider when shopping for health coverage.

Three deductible levels let members choose a plan that fits their financial situation. Someone with a larger emergency fund might prefer a higher deductible to reduce monthly costs.

Another person might prefer paying more each month in exchange for a lower deductible. The key is choosing a plan that fits both your budget and your ability to handle unexpected medical expenses.

Solo Health provides access to the MultiPlan PHCS network, which includes participating providers across all 50 states.

This may be especially valuable for entrepreneurs who travel frequently or work in multiple locations. Members can also seek out-of-network care, although additional financial risks can apply.

Unlike limited-benefit programs, Solo Health advertises coverage for major medical expenses such as hospital stays, surgeries, and emergency care.

It also includes preventive care, prescription benefits, and mental health services. The company states that there are no annual or lifetime dollar caps on covered medical benefits.

Solo Health’s business-based structure may offer tax advantages for eligible business owners. The company states that monthly plan costs are generally deductible as a business expense.

However, the tax treatment depends on your business structure and individual circumstances. Consult a qualified tax professional before assuming your payments will qualify for a deduction.

Eligible preventive services are covered at 100% from the beginning of coverage. This feature helps people prioritize preventive care while managing overall medical expenses.

While Solo Health has appealing features, it also has important limitations.

Solo Health requires applicants to have an eligible business with an active EIN. Applicants must also complete a health questionnaire.

If you don’t meet the company’s participation requirements, you may not qualify for coverage. This makes Solo Health less accessible than ACA Marketplace coverage, which generally offers guaranteed issue during applicable enrollment periods.

A $10,000 deductible may be manageable for someone with substantial savings. However, it could create financial hardship for someone living paycheck to paycheck.

Before selecting a high-deductible plan, make sure you have enough savings to handle unexpected healthcare costs. The lowest monthly payment isn’t necessarily the best financial decision if it exposes you to expenses you cannot afford.

Solo Health uses reference-based pricing for out-of-network services. This means the plan may reimburse a benchmarked amount rather than the provider’s full billed charge.

If the provider charges more than the plan allows, you could be responsible for the difference. This is sometimes called balance billing.

Although Solo Health offers support services to help members navigate medical bills, that does not necessarily eliminate the risk of additional charges.

Solo Health’s enrollment process includes health-related eligibility questions. This differs from ACA-compliant individual health insurance.

If you have ongoing medical conditions or a complicated medical history, review the eligibility requirements carefully.

Accurate answers are essential, and the company states that incomplete or inaccurate information can result in denial of coverage.

Although Solo Health advertises no annual or lifetime dollar caps on covered medical benefits, certain services have visit limits.

For example, outpatient mental health therapy is generally limited to 40 visits annually per covered individual. Some treatments also require prior authorization. Read the complete plan documents so you understand these limitations before enrolling.

Solo Health’s self-funded model may be unfamiliar to people who have only purchased traditional insurance.

The arrangement involves a self-funded business health plan, third-party administration, and a medical reimbursement policy.

Because this structure differs from a standard individual insurance policy, it is worth reviewing the legal and financial responsibilities involved.

How does Solo Health compare with a conventional ACA Marketplace plan?

Traditional ACA Marketplace insurance offers important consumer protections, including guaranteed coverage of preexisting conditions and standardized requirements for essential health benefits.

Solo Health offers a different structure that may appeal to qualifying business owners. However, these products are not interchangeable. For someone with ongoing medical needs, ACA-compliant coverage may provide greater predictability around eligibility and consumer protections.

For an eligible entrepreneur, Solo Health may be worth comparing based on its benefits, provider access, and total annual costs.

Another useful comparison is Solo Health versus healthcare-sharing organizations such as Zion HealthShare. Although both may appeal to people exploring alternatives to conventional individual insurance, they work differently.

Solo Health offers a self-funded major medical plan established through an eligible business.

Its structure includes formal plan documents, medical claims administration, and a self-funded plan structure.

Zion HealthShare is a healthcare-sharing organization. Members contribute monthly amounts to share eligible medical expenses within the community.

Healthcare-sharing programs are not insurance, and they don’t guarantee payment of medical expenses the same way an insurance contract does.

The better option depends on your needs. Solo Health may be more appealing to business owners who want a structured major medical plan with a nationwide provider network.

Zion HealthShare may appeal to people who are comfortable with the healthcare-sharing model and its guidelines. Don’t choose either based on monthly costs alone. Consider the eligibility requirements, exclusions, payment structure, and your financial exposure if you experience a major medical event.

Solo Health may be worth considering for:

It may be particularly appealing to someone who wants to explore a business-based health plan rather than purchasing coverage through the individual insurance market.

If you have significant ongoing medical expenses, compare your options carefully.

If you’re interested in Solo Health, you can start the enrollment process online.

Make sure you have an eligible business with an active EIN. Review the company’s health eligibility requirements before proceeding.

Visit Solo Health’s website and enter the information requested. Your quote will depend on your individual circumstances.

Review the three available plan designs. Consider both the monthly cost and what you might have to pay if you need significant medical care.

Answer the required health questions accurately. Enrollment is subject to approval.

Before completing enrollment, carefully review the plan’s Summary Plan Description, exclusions, and payment terms.

Once approved and enrolled, you can access your plan information through the member portal.

Solo Health operates a business-based, self-funded major medical plan with a defined administrative structure. However, a documented plan structure does not independently verify financial strength, claims performance, or customer satisfaction.

Prospective members should review the legal documents and verify the applicable entities and regulatory disclosures.

Solo Health requires a health questionnaire to determine eligibility. Unlike ACA Marketplace plans, enrollment is not guaranteed regardless of medical history.

Ask the company how its eligibility rules and plan terms apply to your specific circumstances.

Yes. Solo Health allows eligible business owners to include qualifying family members.

The company publishes family aggregate deductibles equal to twice the individual deductible.

Possibly. Solo Health uses the MultiPlan PHCS network.

Verify that your doctor participates in and accepts your specific plan before enrolling. Out-of-network care may be available, but additional charges can apply.

Solo Health generally allows members to choose a different deductible at renewal.

Mid-year changes require approval and may affect the monthly cost.

They may be deductible depending on your business structure and tax situation.

Consult your tax professional for guidance.

Solo Health advertises access to participating providers in all 50 states.

However, nationwide provider access does not necessarily mean every applicant or business can enroll in every state.

Confirm availability and eligibility directly with the company.

Solo Health offers an interesting alternative for self-employed individuals seeking major medical coverage outside the traditional individual insurance market. Its biggest advantages include multiple deductible options, access to a nationwide PPO network, preventive care benefits, and coverage for significant medical expenses.

For qualifying entrepreneurs, the business-based structure may also provide financial and tax-planning opportunities. However, there are important trade-offs. Applicants must meet health eligibility requirements, higher deductibles can create substantial out-of-pocket costs, and out-of-network billing can become complicated.

I recommend comparing Solo Health with at least two other coverage options before deciding. Look beyond the monthly payment and calculate what you might spend over an entire year, including deductibles, prescription costs, and potential out-of-network expenses.

The goal isn’t simply to find the cheapest health plan. It’s to find coverage that protects your health and your finances when you need it most. Eligible self-employed business owners may want to explore Solo Health.

#8482. Zoe Financial Review – Free Matches With Vetted Fiduciaries, if You Have $150,000

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Use Zoe Financial if you have $150,000 or more to invest and want screened fiduciary advisors to interview at no cost. The advisor you hire pays Zoe, and the SEC fined it in 2026 for not fully disclosing why some advisors got its referrals, so check each match’s fees and record yourself.

Picking a financial advisor means trusting a stranger with your savings, and the title alone tells you nothing about their training, their fees, or who else pays them. Zoe Financial screens advisors for you and sets up calls with as many as three of them at no charge, because the advisor you hire pays Zoe instead.

Zoe is a New York investment adviser, formed in 2016 and registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) since 2019. Its founder and CEO, Andres Garcia-Amaya, holds the Chartered Financial Analyst (CFA) charter and was a global market strategist at J.P. Morgan Asset Management. Zoe began matching people with advisors in 2018 and now runs that service at FindAnAdvisor.com as the Zoe Network. In 2023 and 2024 the network held between about 128 and 225 advisory firms, by the SEC’s count. Its Trustpilot profile shows a 4.7 rating from 92 reviews, six of them from the past year. In September 2026, Zoe settled SEC charges over how it disclosed the conflicts behind its referrals.

Zoe’s service has three parts: the match, the screening behind it, and the investing platform Zoe’s advisors use for clients’ accounts. Matching and screening cost you nothing, but Zoe charges fees on the platform that can land on your bill.

A two-minute form asks about your household income, your goals, what you own, and your ZIP code. Zoe’s algorithm then suggests up to three advisors, and you book free calls to interview them, though Zoe’s SEC brochure notes that some people get a single name.

A concierge team books the calls and looks for a better fit if the first names miss. You’re never obligated to hire anyone, and most advisors in the network work remotely, so where you live doesn’t narrow the list.

The form doesn’t weigh your tolerance for risk or your full finances, the brochure says, so the calls are where you judge fit.

Zoe sets no minimum to use the form, but its advisors take clients with at least $150,000 in investable assets and $100,000 in income, and some set a higher bar. Its average client has more than $750,000. With less to invest, a robo-advisor, an automated service that manages a fund portfolio for a small yearly fee, usually fits better. So do the kinds of advisors paid a flat fee or by the hour, whose fees don’t grow with your portfolio.

Zoe says every advisor in its network holds a Certified Financial Planner (CFP) certification, the CFA charter, or a certified public accountant (CPA) license, with five or more years of experience and a clean SEC record. Each is a fiduciary, legally bound to put your interests first, and Zoe says its matches don’t sell commission-paying products, such as some annuities and insurance policies.

Its SEC brochure describes a looser test. Zoe checks that a firm centers on financial planning, that some of its advisors hold a credential such as the CFA, CFP, or CPA, or a graduate business degree, and that it has no material disciplinary history. It reviews each advisor’s regulatory filings and rereads every firm’s brochure once a year.

What Zoe doesn’t check is how an advisor performs once you’ve hired one. Before your first call, look up each match’s record yourself. Ask, too, whether the advisor is fee-only, paid by you alone, since not every fiduciary is.

Zoe’s third step, after the form and the calls, is opening your accounts on its investing platform, launched in 2023. Advisors in its referral program join by invitation and must keep a minimum level of client assets there, so expect the advisor you hire to suggest it.

Those are brokerage accounts held by Apex Clearing, which keeps the assets and settles the trades, and opened through Zoe’s sister brokerage, Zoe Securities. Trades in stocks, exchange-traded funds (ETFs), and mutual funds carry no commission. Your advisor can choose ready-made model portfolios from firms such as BlackRock, Vanguard, and State Street. The platform rebalances them automatically and can harvest tax losses, selling investments at a loss to offset taxable gains.

The accounts are yours, so leaving an advisor means moving them to another firm or hiring another advisor who uses Zoe’s platform.

Zoe doesn’t publish what its advisors charge, so the fee schedule each match hands you is the number to compare.

Zoe’s site says you won’t pay to use its platform, while its client relationship summary, filed with the SEC, says you or your advisor will. Ask each match to put every fee, Zoe’s included, on the agreement you sign.

Say a match charges 1% a year, the rate Zoe’s own fee guide uses in its examples. On $150,000, that’s $1,500 a year, and on $750,000, it’s $7,500, before fund expenses or platform fees.

Zoe’s satisfaction guarantee is narrower than its FAQ makes it sound. The FAQ promises a refund of all advisor fees if you’re unhappy, but the terms cap it at one billing period of fees, a month’s or a quarter’s worth. You qualify only after three months of full advisory service, must ask within a 24-month window between hiring and leaving the advisor, and get nothing back for one-time or hourly planning.

When you hire a match, that advisor pays Zoe 15% to 35% of the fee it charges you, Zoe’s solicitation disclosure says. Zoe collects that share for as long as you stay when the fee is a percentage of your assets, and for five years of a flat-fee planning arrangement. Some advisors pay a one-time referral fee instead. On a $7,500 yearly fee, Zoe’s share would come to $1,125 to $2,625 a year.

Zoe’s contracts bar advisors from charging referred clients more, so you’d pay the same fee walking in on your own. To screen advisors yourself, the National Association of Personal Financial Advisors (NAPFA) keeps an online directory of fee-only advisors you can sort by how they charge.

That pay gives Zoe reasons to favor some advisors. Its share differs by firm, and some advisors pay just to join the network. Several advisory firms, Creative Planning and Mariner Wealth Advisors among them, own small stakes in Zoe, and some of its owners are in the network. Zoe’s own advisory arm competes for the same referrals, and Zoe earns platform fees from advisors who use its platform. Zoe says its algorithm weighs none of this.

The SEC found that referrals didn’t always work that way. In a settled order of September 28, 2026, the agency said that in 2023 and 2024 Zoe didn’t tell users it had a financial stake in steering them to advisors using its new platform. As that period went on, Zoe told advisors who wouldn’t adopt the platform that they’d be dropped from the network. It also found that Zoe’s statement that referrals rested solely on users’ answers was misleading, since salespeople often suggested other advisors. Clients who hired a network advisor in that period picked one the algorithm hadn’t first suggested about 46% of the time.

Zoe agreed, without admitting or denying the findings, to be censured, to stop such violations, and to pay a $450,000 penalty. It says it has since told salespeople not to recommend advisors of their own and hired a full-time chief compliance officer. Ask whoever books your calls how each advisor made your list.

Zoe Financial is a sound starting point for anyone with $150,000 or more who wants a fiduciary advisor and doesn’t know where to begin. It narrows the field to screened, credentialed firms, books the interviews, and costs you nothing, and its contracts keep its cut of your advisor’s fee off your bill.

It’s a poor fit below that bar, and for anyone who wants a referral with no money riding on the outcome, since Zoe earns more from some advisors than others and the SEC found it didn’t fully disclose that. Treat each match as a candidate, not a recommendation. Ask why the advisor made your list, get the full fee schedule in writing with any platform fees on it, and check the record before you sign.

Business class hops across Europe for fewer points than most domestic economy awards

Picture this: you've just crossed the Atlantic on a long-haul award, touched down at London Heathrow, and now you need to get to Rome for the real adventure to begin. Most travelers at this point resign themselves to a cramped economy seat on a budget carrier, dragging luggage through a secondary terminal. But you? You're walking into the Virgin Atlantic clubhouse, sipping a Bloody Mary, and then settling into a proper business class seat for the 2.5-hour hop to Fiumicino. That's the magic of this redemption. Here's the math that should make your jaw drop. A business class seat on a short-haul European flight — London Heathrow to Rome, London to Athens, London to virtually any major European city — routinely retails for **$1,000 to $3,000 in cash**. Airlines know that business travelers on these routes are often on corporate accounts and will pay whatever it costs. The leisure traveler simply doesn't book business class on a two-hour flight because it feels absurd. And that's exactly the pricing inefficiency the ChooseFI community learns to exploit. Virgin Atlantic's Flying Club prices these short-haul European business class seats at a flat **17,500 miles one-way**. At the low end of that $1,000–$3,000 cash range, you're already extracting **5.7 cents per point** — well above what most programs deliver. At the high end, when those seats spike to $3,000 on peak travel dates, you're looking at a staggering **17.1 cents per point**. For context, most travel rewards experts consider 1.5–2 cents per point a solid redemption. This one can deliver *ten times* that. What makes this feel particularly right for the FI mindset is the positioning angle. This isn't just a standalone splurge — it's the finishing move on a transatlantic trip you've already largely funded with points. You've landed in London. You need to get to your final European destination. Instead of paying $200 for a budget airline seat that charges extra for your carry-on, you drop 17,500 Virgin miles and arrive refreshed, fed, and ready. The opportunity cost of those miles is low; the experiential upgrade is enormous. This is what travel rewards done right looks like: not flying business class because you're wealthy, but because you understood the system better than the airlines expected you to.

The core insight here is understanding how Virgin Atlantic prices its own metal versus partner awards — and then deliberately choosing the right one for the right job.

Virgin Atlantic's Flying Club is famous in the points community for two things. First, its partner award sweet spots: ANA First Class for as low as 55,000–60,000 miles one-way, Delta One at competitive rates. These are the headline acts. But quietly sitting in the same award chart is a genuinely underappreciated gem — Virgin's own short-haul European business class, priced at a flat 17,500 miles regardless of the specific route within that distance band.

Why does Virgin price it this way? Virgin Atlantic operates as a premium carrier and sets its award chart to reflect aspirational redemptions — the kind that make Flying Club membership feel worthwhile. For long-haul routes on their own metal, their pricing is competitive but not exceptional. For short-haul Europe, however, the fixed pricing creates an opportunity: a two-hour flight to Rome or Athens costs the same 17,500 miles as a cheaper, shorter hop, but those premium routes have cash prices that routinely spike into the thousands. The chart wasn't built to be a loophole — it's just that cash prices for short-haul business class in Europe are genuinely volatile and often extraordinary.

The fuel surcharge reality check. Here's where you need to pay close attention. Virgin Atlantic is known for passing fuel surcharges onto award redemptions on their own flights. This is the opposite of what happens on ANA or Delta partner awards booked through Flying Club (which carry zero surcharges). On a short-haul European route, those surcharges are real but typically far more manageable than on a transatlantic segment — often in the $50–$150 range rather than $500+. The CPP math still works strongly in your favor, but you should go in with eyes open: this is not a zero-cash-outlay redemption.

The transfer path is exceptional. This is where the ChooseFI community has a serious structural advantage. Virgin Atlantic Flying Club accepts transfers from essentially every major points currency:

Every major transferable currency gets you there at a 1:1 ratio with instant speed. That means if you're holding Chase points from your Sapphire Reserve or Preferred, Amex points from your Gold or Platinum, or Citi points from your Premier card, you have a direct, frictionless pipeline to 17,500 Virgin miles within minutes of finding availability. This is critical because, as you'll learn in the booking section, Virgin availability on its own short-haul European routes can be limited, and you want to be able to move fast when a seat opens up.

The booking window opens 331 days in advance — use it. Miles don't expire as long as you have account activity within 36 months, so there's no pressure to burn them before you're ready.

Before you touch a single website, clarify your mission: you're looking for Virgin Atlantic-operated business class availability on short-haul European routes departing from London Heathrow (LHR). This is not a search for partner award space — this is VS metal, VS availability, VS seats. Your most common target routes will be LHR → FCO (Rome), LHR → ATH (Athens), and similar European city pairs. Build your itinerary around where VS actually flies in Europe, not every possible destination.

Go to virginatlantic.com and use the award search tool. Select "Book with miles" and enter your route. Virgin shows its own availability directly here — you don't need a third-party search engine for this specific redemption. Search one-way rather than round-trip so you can see each direction independently. If your target dates show no availability, flex by ±3 days. Business class award seats on short-haul routes are typically released in small batches.

Open a second browser tab and search the same route and date on Google Flights or directly on virginatlantic.com for a revenue ticket. Note the cash price for business class. This is your CPP sanity check — if the cash price is $1,200 and you're spending 17,500 miles plus ~$100 in surcharges, you're at roughly 6.3 cents per point. If the cash price is $2,500, your CPP jumps dramatically. This step helps you prioritize which dates to target.

Log into your Virgin Atlantic Flying Club account. If you don't have 17,500 miles already, check your transferable points balances:

Do NOT transfer points until you have confirmed award availability on your target date. Transfers to Virgin are one-directional and cannot be reversed.

Once you've confirmed a seat is available, transfer your points from your chosen program. For Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt transfers, the miles land in your Flying Club account instantly. Refresh your Flying Club account, confirm the miles are there, and complete the booking before the seat disappears. Enter your payment details for the taxes and surcharges (typically $50–$150 on short-haul European routes).

If you're struggling to find seats close to your travel dates, shift your strategy to the booking window's leading edge. Virgin opens award availability 331 days in advance. Set a calendar reminder 331 days before your ideal travel date, log in at that exact time, and book the moment inventory releases. Peak-season seats to popular destinations like Rome and Athens move quickly.

After booking, screenshot your confirmation, note your booking reference, and verify the routing, cabin class, and surcharge amounts. Add the flight to your calendar with the Virgin Atlantic booking reference. Sign up for flight notifications.

Virgin Atlantic operates its own short-haul flights from London Heathrow to destinations across Europe including Amsterdam, Paris, Edinburgh, Geneva, and Athens. These are different from partner codeshare flights. The 17,500-point price applies specifically to Virgin Atlantic-operated short-haul business class. Partner flights (booked through Flying Club but operated by Delta, KLM, or Air France) use a different award chart and typically cost significantly more. When searching, filter for Virgin Atlantic flight numbers (VS prefix) to find the sweet spot pricing. The business class product on short-haul includes a dedicated cabin, lounge access at Heathrow, priority boarding, and meal service.

Card links may earn ChooseFI a commission. See our advertiser disclosure.

Let's walk through a real scenario that illustrates exactly what this redemption looks like in practice.

The Setup: You've just arrived at London Heathrow on a transatlantic award — perhaps an ANA First Class redemption through the very same Flying Club program. You have a few days in London, and now you need to get to Athens, Greece, where your Mediterranean adventure begins. You check flights: a business class seat on Virgin Atlantic's LHR → ATH route on your target date is priced at $2,200 cash.

The Redemption: You log into virginatlantic.com and find a business class award seat on that same flight: 17,500 Virgin miles + approximately $120 in taxes and fuel surcharges. You have 20,000 Citi ThankYou Points sitting in your ThankYou account from your Citi Premier card. You initiate the transfer — 1:1, instant — and within minutes, your Flying Club account reflects 17,500 miles (with 2,500 to spare for future use). You complete the booking.

The Experience: On the day of travel, you access the Virgin Clubhouse at Heathrow — one of the most celebrated airport lounges in the world. The cocktail bar, the à la carte dining, the spa treatments available before departure — this is the part that makes the ChooseFI community members shake their heads in disbelief when they first experience it. Then you board and settle into Virgin's short-haul business class: a proper dedicated seat, a full meal service, attentive cabin crew. For a two-and-a-half-hour flight, it's a genuinely elevated experience.

You land in Athens refreshed, fed, and without having spent thousands of dollars. That's the positioning flight done right — and it's what separates travelers who understand the travel rewards system from those who are still paying cash for European business class.

Do this: Use it as a positioning flight on a broader trip This redemption was practically designed for trip architecture. If you're already planning a transatlantic journey — coming into London on a long-haul award — the 17,500-mile European hop becomes the natural, high-value conclusion. You're not just booking a short flight; you're completing a fully points-funded journey across two continents. Think of this as the last domino.

Do this: Search 331 days out for peak season Virgin's booking window opens exactly 331 days before departure. For summer travel to Athens, Rome, or other peak European destinations, business class award inventory gets claimed early. Set a phone reminder 331 days before your ideal travel date. Log in that morning. The seats that seem impossible to find in the 60-day window are often available the moment the calendar rolls over.

Do this: Compare cash prices before transferring Not all dates are created equal. A Tuesday in November to Rome might retail for $800 in business class — still a reasonable 4.6 CPP — while the same route on a Friday in July might hit $2,800, delivering 17+ CPP. Run the cash price check on Google Flights before you commit your miles. Target the high-cash-price windows for maximum value extraction.

Avoid this: Transferring points before confirming availability This is the single most common mistake. Transferring miles to Virgin Atlantic is a one-way street. If you send 17,500 Chase points over and then discover the seat isn't actually available (or you misread the cabin class), those miles are stuck in Flying Club. Always — always — confirm the specific flight and cabin availability first, THEN transfer.

Avoid this: Confusing this with partner award bookings Virgin's zero-surcharge policy applies to partner airlines like ANA and Delta. On Virgin Atlantic-operated flights (which this redemption is), expect fuel surcharges of $50–$150. Budget for these. They don't destroy the CPP math, but they're a genuine cash cost you need to plan around.

Do this: Hold Virgin miles for multiple redemptions Because miles don't expire with account activity every 36 months, there's no reason to hoard and rush. Keep Flying Club active by earning miles through their shopping portal or partners, and wait for the right route and cash price moment to pounce.

This redemption is built for a specific type of ChooseFI traveler: the intermediate-to-advanced points strategist who thinks in itineraries, not individual flights.

The ideal candidate is someone who's already planning a trip that routes through London Heathrow — perhaps on a transatlantic award — and needs an elegant, high-value way to reach their final European destination. Solo travelers and couples benefit most here. At 17,500 miles per person, a couple needs 35,000 Virgin miles, which is completely achievable with a single transfer from a combined Chase or Amex balance.

Families should approach with caution. This redemption scores a 2/5 for family-friendliness for good reason. Multiplying 17,500 miles per person across four or more travelers creates a significant points requirement, and availability for multiple seats on the same flight is far from guaranteed. The fuel surcharges also multiply with passenger count. Families are better served by other redemption strategies.

This is NOT for beginners. The overall score of 2.7/5 and beginner-friendliness rating of 1/5 signal real complexity. If you're just starting your travel rewards journey, build your foundation with simpler redemptions first. But if you've got a year of points accumulation behind you and you're ready to think architecturally about trip planning, this sweet spot can be a revelatory experience.

This redemption is rated **Hard** — and that rating is earned honestly. The difficulty isn't in the math or the concept; it's in three very real execution challenges. **Challenge 1: Finding award availability.** Virgin Atlantic doesn't release enormous quantities of business class award seats on its own short-haul European flights. You may search a dozen dates before finding a seat. This is the primary friction point. The fix: use the 331-day advance booking window religiously, and be genuinely flexible on your travel dates by at least ±3 days. **Challenge 2: Navigating the Virgin Atlantic booking interface.** Compared to programs like Chase's travel portal, Flying Club's award search tool is clunkier and less intuitive. It occasionally shows availability that isn't actually bookable through to completion. The fix: search virginatlantic.com directly, be patient with the interface, and have your payment information ready to move quickly when a seat surfaces. **Challenge 3: Understanding the surcharge reality.** New points enthusiasts sometimes expect zero out-of-pocket on award bookings. Virgin's fuel surcharges on its own metal are real, and they'll surprise you if you're not expecting them. The fix: budget $50–$150 per person in cash costs as a baseline assumption. The good news: the **transfer path is as easy as it gets** in the points world. Instant 1:1 transfers from Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt mean that once you find availability, you can have miles in your account and a booking confirmed in under 10 minutes. If you're willing to invest the search time and approach with patience, this is one of those redemptions that fundamentally changes how you see the travel rewards system. The payoff — business class in Europe for 17,500 miles — is worth the effort.

This redemption works best as part of a larger trip. If you are flying transatlantic to or from Europe, route through London Heathrow. Then use the short-haul award to connect to your final European destination at a fraction of the cost of a separate ticket.

Log into VirginAtlantic.com and search for reward flights in Upper Class (business) on your desired European route. Look for VS-coded flights only. Ignore partner-operated results, which will price differently.

Midweek flights (Tuesday through Thursday) and shoulder season dates offer the best availability. Peak summer weekends and holiday periods are harder to find. Build flexibility into your schedule if possible.

Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers to Flying Club are instant, making Chase the preferred transfer partner for time-sensitive bookings. Amex Membership Rewards also transfers 1:1 but may take 1-2 days.

Complete the booking on VirginAtlantic.com. Your business class ticket includes access to the Virgin Atlantic Clubhouse at Heathrow, one of the best airport lounges in Europe. Arrive early and enjoy it as part of the experience.

Virgin Atlantic operates short-haul flights from London Heathrow to destinations including Amsterdam, Paris CDG, Edinburgh, Geneva, Athens, Tel Aviv, and several others. Routes change seasonally, so check VirginAtlantic.com for current schedules. The 17,500-point sweet spot applies to all Virgin Atlantic-operated short-haul business class flights.

Yes, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club prices awards as one-way, so you can book a single short-haul business class segment for 17,500 points. This makes it ideal for positioning flights where you only need one direction covered by points.

The flight itself is short, but the value extends beyond the seat. You get dedicated check-in, priority boarding, the Heathrow Clubhouse lounge (which is excellent), a meal service, and a more relaxed travel experience. At 17,500 points, the per-point value (3-5 cents) makes it a strong redemption even for a short flight.

Virgin Atlantic does add taxes and fees to award tickets, including some carrier-imposed surcharges. On short-haul European routes, total out-of-pocket costs typically run $50-$150 depending on the route and departure airport taxes. This is higher than some programs but still reasonable given the business class product.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

The Virgin Atlantic short-haul European business class sweet spot is the perfect complement to a transatlantic award trip. At just 17,500 points, it costs less than most domestic economy awards while delivering business class service, Heathrow Clubhouse lounge access, and a stress-free connection to destinations across Europe. It is not the flashiest redemption in travel rewards, but it is one of the most practical: a building block that makes multi-city European itineraries accessible and affordable for the FI community.

#8479. Kraken Review – One Account for Crypto, Stocks & Pro Trading

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Open a Kraken account if you want crypto, U.S. stocks, and pro-grade trading under one login, from an exchange that publishes proof of reserves. Place your regular buys on Kraken Pro rather than the app, whose 1% fee and built-in spread make it the account’s costliest way to trade.

Buying crypto in a simple app is easy but costly. Trading on an exchange’s order book, the live list of buy and sell offers, costs less but takes more know-how, and stocks usually sit at a separate brokerage. Kraken puts all three behind one login, so the decision that matters is where you place each trade.

Kraken is the trading name of Payward Inc., founded in 2011, and it says more than 13 million people worldwide trust it. In the U.S., it’s licensed to transfer customers’ money in 46 jurisdictions and offers stock trading through Kraken Securities, a broker-dealer registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). It also publishes proof-of-reserves reviews, which check that it holds the crypto its clients’ balances show, a practice it says it began in 2014.

The account has five parts: a simple app, a pro exchange, stock trading, ways to earn on idle coins, and two companion apps.

The Kraken app is the simple side of the account. You buy, sell, or convert crypto at the price it quotes, set recurring buys daily, weekly, or monthly on more than 200 coins, and pay by bank transfer, debit card, or PayPal. Kraken says it lists more than 600 cryptocurrencies, though it restricts 83 of them for U.S. clients. The app suits investors who buy now and then and don’t want to learn an order book.

Kraken Pro, on the same login, is the full exchange, with stop-loss and take-profit orders, charts with 25-plus trading and data widgets, a desktop app, and API access for your own trading software. Eligible U.S. traders can also trade on margin, borrowing against their crypto for positions worth up to 20 times their collateral on some coins, and trade perpetual futures, contracts with no expiration date. Both run through Kraken Derivatives US, a futures broker registered with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), and Kraken warns that margin losses can exceed what you put up.

The Kraken app and Kraken Pro also trade more than 11,000 U.S.-listed stocks and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) with no commission, through Kraken Securities, in every state Kraken serves. Orders placed outside market hours wait for the next session, Kraken Pro adds trading 24 hours a day on weekdays, and Kraken charges nothing on its end to move shares in from another broker.

Once you switch it on, Auto Earn stakes eligible idle coins, committing them to help run their blockchains in return for rewards. It pays weekly and keeps the coins free to trade or withdraw, and on coins that make you wait to unstake, it pays rewards on up to half of what you stake. Bonded staking pays more for locking coins up for a set term.

Rates on the biggest coins are low. Kraken estimates Auto Earn’s annual percentage yield (APY) at 0.02% for bitcoin and 1.47% for ether, before its commission. DeFi Earn puts USDC, a stablecoin pegged to the dollar, into vaults that lend it on blockchain lending markets for up to 5.33% APY, though the rate floats, the product isn’t regulated, and you can lose money.

Kraken Wallet is a free self-custody app, meaning you hold the keys to your coins instead of Kraken, on Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, and other networks. Krak, a separate money app, sends money free between Kraken users and lets you spend through the Krak Card, a Visa debit card from Lead Bank. The card pays up to 2% cash back, at a rate set by the average assets you hold across Krak, Kraken, and Kraken Pro, and because Krak isn’t a bank, its balances carry no FDIC deposit insurance.

The app’s convenience is the account’s biggest cost. Every app price includes a spread, a markup over the market rate that Kraken doesn’t publish and may keep, on top of these fees.

Counting fees alone, since Kraken doesn’t publish the app’s spread, here is what $500 of bitcoin a month costs by our math. The app charges $5 a month, or $60 a year. Kraken+ costs $59.88 a year on monthly billing, so it pays off once app trades top about $500 a month, or about $417 on the annual plan. Kraken Pro charges $2 for the same buy as a maker order or $4 as a taker order, and Kraken says Pro prices carry no hidden spread.

If you want only bitcoin or ether as a long-term slice of a portfolio, a spot exchange-traded product (ETP) is the main alternative. It holds the coin itself and trades on a stock exchange, so you skip the crypto wallet and keys, though you pay the fund’s sponsor an ongoing fee that direct holders don’t.

Kraken says no custodial wallet it manages has been breached since its founding in 2011, and it keeps most client crypto offline, in cold storage in guarded facilities. Accounts sign in with passkeys and two-factor authentication and can’t be recovered by text message.

An independent accountant’s proof-of-reserves review for Sept. 30, 2026, found Kraken held 103.2% of its clients’ bitcoin and 100.7% of their ether. Kraken notes that such a review can’t rule out hidden claims on the coins or prove they weren’t borrowed, and it covers only the coins it names, not dollar balances.

Crypto at Kraken carries neither FDIC deposit insurance nor the brokerage protection of the Securities Investor Protection Corporation (SIPC). Stocks are different. Kraken Securities is a member, and SIPC covers up to $500,000, including $250,000 in cash, if a member brokerage fails, though never market losses.

Kraken’s record with regulators is mixed. In 2023 it paid $30 million to settle SEC charges over its old U.S. staking program and shut that program down, relaunching U.S. staking as a new product in 2025. A separate SEC lawsuit claiming Kraken ran an unregistered securities exchange was dismissed for good in 2025.

Kraken serves every state except New York and Maine, and some features run on shorter lists. Staking is open only in 37 states, Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico, which by our count leaves out 11 states Kraken otherwise serves, including California, Texas, Illinois, and New Jersey. The Krak Card isn’t offered in Massachusetts or Indiana, and Krak’s cash transfers aren’t available in Indiana, Louisiana, Massachusetts, or Utah. Margin and perpetual futures go only to traders who meet Kraken’s eligibility rules.

Support runs around the clock by live chat and email, with phone calls only in select cases. Kraken calls you only after you’ve contacted it and arranged the call, so treat any other call, or a Kraken number found in a search ad, as a scam. Of Kraken’s 9,583 reviews on Trustpilot, 49% give one star and 33% give five, for a TrustScore of 3.1 out of 5.

Kraken is a strong pick for investors who want crypto, U.S. stocks, and serious trading tools in one account. Its best case is Kraken Pro’s low fees beside the beginner app, backed by proof of reserves and a clean custody record.

It’s the wrong account for New York and Maine residents, who can’t open one, and for anyone in the 11 other states without staking who wants rewards on idle coins. Long-term holders who want only bitcoin or ether can own them through a spot ETP instead. Everyone else should open the account and route regular buys through Kraken Pro, or add Kraken+ once app trades top about $500 a month.

#8478. Monarch Money Review – Every Household Account in One Shared App, for $99.99 a Year

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Pay for Monarch Money if you want your household’s budget, bills, investments, and net worth in one app you and a partner both use, since a partner joins the $99.99-a-year Core plan free. Skip Plus, at $199.99, unless you’ll use its retirement forecasts or track a side business.

A household’s money rarely sits in one place: checking at one bank, credit cards at others, a 401(k) through work, a mortgage, and a partner with accounts of their own. Monarch Money pulls those accounts into one app that you and a partner can each log in to, and it charges a subscription instead of showing ads.

Monarch Money’s CEO, Val Agostino, was among the first product managers at Mint, the free budgeting app Intuit later shut down. He started the company in 2019 alongside Ozzie Osman and Jon Sutherland. The company now calls its app simply Monarch, and by October 2026 it had more than 1 million members. The app holds 4.9 stars from about 119,000 ratings on Apple’s App Store and 4.8 stars from about 26,000 reviews on Google Play.

Monarch sells two plans, Core and Plus. Everything in this section comes with Core, and the pricing section below covers what Plus adds.

Monarch offers two ways to budget, and you can switch between them. Flex budgeting, the default, sorts expenses into fixed, flexible, and non-monthly groups and has you watch one number, the flexible spending you have left this month. Category budgeting sets a limit for each category, such as groceries or dining out. Either way, Monarch drafts your first budget from your last six months of spending.

It builds each month’s budget on the income you expect, while YNAB has you budget only money that has already arrived. Leftover money in a category can roll over to the next month, which is how Monarch handles once-a-year bills, and alerts warn you before you overspend.

Transactions arrive already sorted into categories, and rules let you correct what the sorting gets wrong. As transactions come in, a rule can match on the merchant, amount, category, or account, then rename the merchant, change the category, add tags, split the charge, or hide it from your budget. The Recurring page finds bills and subscriptions in your history and shows them as a calendar or a list, with reminders before each charge.

Monarch tracks each investment you hold, not just account balances, across stocks, mutual funds, exchange-traded funds, 401(k)s, and crypto. It shows how your portfolio splits among stocks, bonds, cash, and other assets and how it has done against the S&P 500. It can also track equity compensation, the stock or options your employer pays you.

Net worth, what you own minus what you owe, refreshes as your linked balances and market prices change. A home’s value can come from Zillow’s estimate and a car’s from VinAudit, crypto can link straight from Coinbase, and anything else goes in as a manual account. U.S. members can add a VantageScore 3.0 credit score from Equifax, which updates monthly and doesn’t affect your credit.

A save-up goal tells you whether you’re on track from your balance, your target date, and what you plan to add each month. A pay-down goal projects a payoff date for each debt, and its calculator compares the avalanche method, which pays the highest interest rate first, with the snowball method, which pays the smallest balance first. Goals sit inside the budget, so you see what goes to them each month.

Adding a partner costs nothing, and each person gets a separate login under the one subscription. Every member sees every linked account and transaction, though, and Monarch’s help center says accounts and transactions can’t be hidden from one another. You can mark each as shared or as one person’s to filter transactions, reports, and accounts, but the household keeps one budget.

If you pay for your own subscription, you can also give a financial planner a year of access at no extra cost and revoke it anytime. The planner can view and edit what you see but can’t link accounts for you. A planner in Monarch’s professional program can instead pay for your subscription, at $14.99 a month per client.

Reports cover spending, income, and cash flow, and you can filter them by category, merchant, account, tag, or owner and save the views you use. The Sankey report draws your money flowing from income into each spending category, and a weekly recap sums up spending, cash flow, and net worth.

The AI Assistant, available to U.S. members, answers plain-English questions about your own accounts, such as why spending jumped last month, and explains how to use Monarch. Since November 2026, a test version also looks for savings on its own, such as a duplicate subscription charge. You can hide the AI features in settings, but automatic categorization stays on.

Monarch links to more than 13,000 banks and other institutions through three data providers, Plaid, MX, and Finicity, and suggests the one with the strongest connection history for each bank. Since September 2026, you can switch an institution to another provider without losing its history, and a public status page shows each provider’s connection record at popular banks. Monarch’s help center says connection problems nearly always lie between the provider and your bank, and that store-brand credit cards and mortgages are harder to keep connected.

Access is read-only, so Monarch can’t move money, and your bank logins go to the data provider, never to Monarch. Data is encrypted in storage and in transit, sign-ins can require two-factor authentication, and independent auditors have certified Monarch under SOC 2, an outside audit of how a company protects customer data.

Paying monthly comes to $179.88 over 12 months, $79.89 more than the annual price for the same Core plan. Sign up on Monarch’s website rather than through an app store. The WELCOME code works only on annual Core plans Monarch bills directly, and the money-back guarantee, which refunds the unused time on your subscription whenever you ask, doesn’t cover subscriptions bought through Apple’s App Store.

Plus costs $100 more a year and adds four things. Forecasting models your net worth and cash flow decades ahead and tests events like retiring at 55, buying a home, or having a child, with every assumption adjustable. Business tracking keeps an LLC, rental property, or side business apart from your personal money, with a profit-and-loss report for each and tax-prep exports, but no invoicing or payroll. Advanced investment analysis compares holdings with what you paid and breaks funds down by asset class using Morningstar data. Plus also includes a couple’s will from Trust & Will, which Monarch values at $299, once your trial ends.

Plus is worth the extra $100 only if you’ll use the retirement forecasts or track a business in it.

Monarch Money is the budgeting app to pay for when a household wants its budget, bills, investments, and net worth together in one app that two people can share. Its strongest case is a couple who keep some accounts separate but want one view of all of them, especially when one partner invests and wants holdings tracked beside the budget. For most of them, Core at $99.99 a year is all they need to buy.

It’s the wrong pick for anyone who wants spending tracked free, and YNAB suits budgeters who want to plan only money already in their accounts. Partners who want any account kept private should look elsewhere too. Everyone else should start the 7-day trial on Monarch’s website, not in an app store, so the WELCOME code and the money-back guarantee both apply. Link every account your household has during the trial, then pay for the year with the code to take 30% off.

Learn more about Monarch Money or see how it compares to the best budgeting apps.
